FROM THE CREEK NATION. Columbus, (Geo.) June 7. Hostile Creeks. þÿ The force of the hostile foe in Alabama has been so variously estimated, that we have taken some pains to ascertain their true members. There are in the Creek nation 8,000 (low estimate) warriors, including boys capable of doing much mischief. There are 700 friendly Indians in th" camps of Opothle Yoho-la and E che I lad jo, 30<i in Chambers county, 80 at this place and 20 at Fort Mitchell ; making in ail 1,100 friendly warriors The Indians have all been repeatedly invited to come in ; their hostility has been put upon this issue, and every inducement ofiered to bring them under our protection Ne-ah Mic-co has 700 warriors at Wa-loota ha-ka, and is, by some, thought " to be friendly ; but such is not the case. General Woodward expressed to us no doubts of his hostility þÿ and we perused a letter a few days since wiitten at Ne-ah þÿMic-co camp, s which detailed nothing but a long series of the most wanttm and blood-thirsty actions. There can be no doubt that the murderous attack on the stages was made hy a band from his camp, some of the stage horses having been found in their possession. After the most thorough inquiry upon tho subject, we cannot but believe that the hostile paity number less than six thousand. To prevent these savage- from escaping into Florida, and to chastise it. m in tlenr <m u country, will require a large force ; ihe former object is of great moment. Should many reach Florida, it is impossible to forsee tho
termination of the war; one warrior in Florida being equal, we think, to ten in Alabama.

New States. þÿ The hills for the admission of the new States Michigan and Arkans ,s into the Union having passed the Senate some time since, and having passed the Houm of Representatives without amendment, require no further action on the part of the Serial- As it is understood that they arc satisfactory to the President, the bills may he regarded as laws and tho two states as admitted into the Union, making the number of states twenty six. The state of Michigan is entitled to two members of the House of Representatives, and the state of Arkansas one, who, together with two Senators from each state will take their seats in the rcsjicctive houses at the next session of Congress; making the number of Representatives 243, and that of the Senators 52. Both states will also, of course, take pat t in the next Presidential election adding seven to the number of electors, and making rhe whole number 295. The number which must he given to a candidate to secure his election by the electors will therefore be 148

DEATH OF THE EX-PRESIDENT MADISON. Washington, June 30, 1836. To the Senate and House of Representatives: It becomes my painful duty to announce to you the melancholy intelligence of the death of J AMES MADISON, ex president of the United States. He departed this lire at half past six þÿo clock, on the morning of the 28th instant, full of years and honor. I hasten this communication, in order that Congress may adopt such measures as may be proper to testify their sense of the respect which is due to the memory of one whose life has contributed so essentially to the happiness and glory of his country, and the good of mankind. ANDREW JACKSON.

TEXAS. It gives us much satisfaction to notice, that the report of Mr. Clay in regard to the recognition of Texas, was adopted in the Senate by a unanimous vote. This report says in substance that the Senate recommend to the President to recognise Texas as independent whenever it is made to appear that she is able to sustain herself as such. In other words, the United States will preserve, touching the question at issue between this province and Mexico, that position of neutrality w hich principle and policy alike demand of her ; and without throwing her weight into either scale, will presume that to be the proper position of affairs, which they assume by the force of circumstances, and which they promise permanently to retain. Such a course is conformable to our national dignity and to that respect for existing engagements which is equally imperative on States and on individuals.

The Colony of British Guiana, situated on the Coast of South America, is the richest and most luxuriant of the British West India I Possessions. It extends from the River Corantyne on the East, to the River Pomeroon on the West, a distance of two hundred miles, comprising the districts of Berbice, Demerara, and Essequibo, and including three large Rivers of the same names; the last of which, (the Essequibo.) is twenty miles wide at the mouth, and contains several large and valuable Islands in a high state of Sugar cultivation. Though the Colony extends about two hundred and fifty miles into the interior, the cultivation is chiefly confined to a strip of Land, of four to five miles in depth along the whole line of Coast, and the Banks of the Rivers for about ten miles from their mouths ; and a great portion of this, though of the richest description of alluvial soil, has been neglected from want of a sufficiency of labour to keep the cultivation in proper order. Throughout the whole of this extensive Colony, there are only two Towns or Ports of Shipping, where the whole of the mercantile and financial business of the Colony is transacted, namely: þÿ New Amsterdam, on the River Berbice, containing about two thousand five hundred Inhabitants, where the chief business of that District is transacted, and the Negro Population of which is twenty-one thousand. And Georgetown, on the River Demerara, containing about thirteen thousand Inhabitants, the Seat of Government, and comprising the

whole business of the Districts of Demerara and Essequibo, with a Negro Population of about seventy thousand, and an extensive intercourse with North America and the West India Islands. The greatest portion of the above Negro Population of ninety-one thousand is regularly and daily employed in the production and manufacture of the staple produce of the Colony, of which the following Exports are made annually to Europe, viz : þÿ 75,000 hogsheads of Sugar, value £1,500,000 35.000 puncheons of Rum þÿ 350,000 30.000 casks ol Molasses, þÿ 5110,000 3,300 bales of Cotton, þÿ 45,000 3.300.000 pounds of Coffee þÿ 140,000 Plantations and Cattle sold þÿ 55,000

In England I looked in vain for misery, and all the complaints that 1 heard seemed to me to be partial and exaggerated ; here, no words can express the frightful truth which everywhere meets the eye. To form an idea of it, you must see these houses þÿ not houses but huts þÿ not huts but hovels, mostly without windows or apertures; the same entrance, the same narrow space for men and hogs þÿ the latter lively, sleek, and well fed ; the former covered with rags, or rather hung with fragments rags of in a manner which it is impossible to conceive. If 1 except the respectable people in the towns, I did not see upon thousands of Irish a whole coat, a whole shirt, a whole cloak ; but all in tatters, and tatters such as are nowhere else to be seen. The ruins of ancient castles were pointed out to me ; but how could I take any pleasure in them, while the desolate ruined huts surrounded me, and testified the distress of the present times more loudly than the others did the grandeur of the past ? But then the lords were of the same race, of the same language > they were on the spot, and the people certainly not so wretched as since the confiscations of the English conquerors. Other huts were half fallen down, but the occupants crept into the remaining half, which was not larger than a coffin for the wretched family. When I recollect the well-fed rogues and thieves in the English prisons, I admire, not-

withstanding the very natural increase of Irish criminals, the power of morality : I wonder that the whole nation does not go over and steal, in order to enjoy a new and happier existence. And then the English boast of the good treatment of their countrymen, while the innocent Irish are obliged to live worse than their cattle. In Parliament they talk for years, together, whether it is necessary and becoming to leave 100,000 dollars annually (15,000f.) in the hands of the pastors of 526 Protestants, or 10,759 dollars to the pastors of three Protestants ; while there are thousands here who scarcely know they have a soul, and know nothing of their body, except that it sutlers hunger, thirst, and cold. Which of these ages is the dark and barbarous ; the former, when mendicant monks distributed their goods to the poor, and, in their way, gave them the most rational comfort ; or the latter, when rich (or bankrupt) aristocrates can see the weal of the church and of religion (or of their relations) only in retaining possession of that which was taken and obtained by violence ? All the blame is thrown on agitators, and discontent produced by artificial means þÿ What absurdity 1 Every falling hut causes agitation, and every tattered pair of breeches a sans culntie. Since I have seen Ireland 1 admired the patience and moderation of the people, that they do not (what would be more excusable in them than in distinguished revo lutionists, authors, journalists. Benthamnites, baptized and unbaptized Jews) drive out the
devil through Beelzebub the prince of the devils. þÿ liaumers England in 1835.

Useful Arts. Important to Bakers. þÿ A mechanical kneading-trough has lately been invented by a baker of the name of M. Fontaine, at Paris, for which he has obtained a patent from the French government. The chief advantages derived from this new invention are, that from 300 to 800 pounds of dough can be kneaded in the small space of time of fifteen minutes, with the labour of only one man, and that without the least fatigue. It also causes the dough to be much better kneaded, consequently the bread is much better made than by the process usually adopted. This invention is the fiuit of long experience. Important to Whitesmiths, <$c. þÿ It is perhaps generally not known amongst mechanics that the salt called prussiate of potash, which may be had of all the chemists, is now much used in case-hardening. The process is easy, and saves a great length of time. The method is to powder the salt, and sprinkle it upon the iron when in a state of redness : it will be found to run like oil, and when plunged into cold water, will be found to be as hard or even harder than iron case-hardened in the usual way, Paste made by putting acetate or sugar of lead into it, instead of the old way of mixing it with alum, keeps it from moulding, clear, and quite moist for months together. We have heard that Mr. Hodgson, of Harthburn, communicated this mode of making paste to a book binder in Cursitor street, London, in 1819 ; and that he has found from long experience that it is by far the most useful way he

has ever heard of. Burden's patent horse shoe, of which fifty are made in a minute, are now for sale in most of the hardware stores. Distillation of Salt-water. þÿ P. Nicole of Dieppe, is stated to have succeeded in procuring fresh water from the distillation of sea water, by simply passing the steam of the latter through a stratum of coarsely powderedcharcoal, in its way to the condenser or worm, tub. þÿ London New Monthly.

A parishioner complained to his parson that his pew was too far from the pulpit, and that he must purchase one nearer, " Why," said the parson, " can't you hear distinctly ?" " O yes, I can hear well enough." "Can't you see plainly V "Yes, I can see perfectly well.'1 "Then what can be the trouble/" "Why there are so many in front of me, who catch " what you say first, that by the time your words reach my ears they are as fiat as dishwater." þÿ Boston Post.

7 he following extrordinary case occurred lately in Berwick : þÿ One of the female servants of a respectable family , while engaged in wash ing clothes, received a prick in her hand, with , it was supposed, a needle, which smarted severely at the moment, but the effect seemed soon to pass away, and the circumstance to be almost forgotten. On Saturday morning however, the girl was awoke with an accute pain in the shoulder of which she complained bitterly to her mistress, who, after some consideration, and in vain employing means to as. suage the pain, remembered the pounctute of the needle, and became persuaded it was that which was now occasioning the anguish her servant was suffering. þÿ In the course of the forenoon girl the was sent to the surgeon of the family in question, with a message from her mistress, particularly to examine the part affected, with a view to discover if it was not the needle which had run into the hand, and had now worked its way up to the shoulder and was struggling, as it were, for escape. The surgeon did so, but he saw nothing to lead him to any such conclusion, and sent the girl home with an intimation to that effect. The suffering of the poor girl continuing to increase, and her mistress becoming more and mure persuaded it was nothing but the needle that was the cause of it all, went herself with her servant to the surgeon, upon whom she urged her opinion, and whom she at length induced to make an incision in the shoulder; with a view to discover and extract the needle.

After a painful operation during which the lady, with great firmness, supported her maid in her arms, the forceps were inserted, and at a considerable depth the needle was laid hold of, and drawn outþÿ the identical needle, no doubt, which had punctured the hand several days before, and had gradually made its progress along the whole length of the arm The operation was very skilfully per formed, and relief was soon afforded to the sufferer, who is now almost recovered from the þÿeffects. Berwick Warder.

!»»" - - ' « þÿ-ki« '»-»« " «'' the bazaar of constantinople. Bring all the shops of Now York, Philadelphia, and Boston together around the City Hall ; remove their fronts, pile up their goods on shelves facing the street ; cover the whole with a roof, and metamorphose, your trim clerks into bearded, turbaned, and solemn old Mussulmans, smooth Jews, and calpaokcd and rosy Armenians, and you will have something jike the grand Bazaar of Constantinople. You can scarcely get an idea of it without having been there. It is a city under cover. You walk all day, and day after day, from one street to another, winding and turning, and trudging up hill and down, and never go out of doors. The roof is as high as those of our three-story houses, and the dim light so favorable to shop-keepers comes struggling down through sky-lights never cleaned except by the rains of Heaven. 4 Strolin" O through the bazaar is an endless o amusement. It is slow work, for the streets are as crowded as a church-aisle alter service; and, pushed aside one moment by a bevy of Turkish ladies, shuffling along in their yellow slippers, muffled to the eyes ; the next by a fat slave carrying a child; again by a kr.rvas armed to the teeth, and clearing the way for some coming dignitary, you find your own policy is to draw in your elbows, and suffer the motly crowd to shove you at their pleasure. ' Each shop in this world of traffic may be two yards wide. The owner sits cross-legged on the broad counter below, the heighth ol a

chair from the ground, and hands all you want without stiring from his seat. One broad bench or counter runs the length of the street, and the different shops are only divided by the slight partition of the shelves The purchaser seats himself on the counter, to be out of the way of the crowd, and the shopman spreads out his goods on his knees, never condescending to open his lips except to tell you the price. If he exclaims " bono" or " kalo (the only word a real Turk ever knows o another language), he is stared at by his neighbours as a man would be in Broadway who should breakout with an Italian bravuara. Ten to one while you are examining his goodsf the bearded trader creeps through a hole leading to a kennel of a dormitory in the rear, washes himself and returns to his counter, where, spreading his sacred carpet in the direction of Mecca, he goes through his prayers and prostrations, perfectly unconscious of your presence, or that of the passing crowd. No vocation interferes with his religious duty. Fife times a day if he were running from the plague, the Mussulman would find time lor pravers. The Frank purchaser attracts a great deal of curiosity. As lie points to an embroidered handkerchief, or a rich shawl, or a pair of goldworked slippers, Turkish ladies of the first rank, gathering their ycs/imacks securely over their faces stop close to his side, not minding if they push him a little to get nearer the desired article. Feeling not the least timidity, except for their faces, these true children of

Eve examine the goods in barter, watch the stranger's countenance, and if he takes oil his glove, or pull out his purse, take it up and look at it, without saying " by your leave." Their curiosity often extends to your dress, and they put out their little henna-stained lingers and pass them over the sleeve of your coat with a gurgling expression of admiration at its fineness ; or if you have rings or a watch-guard, they lift up your hands or pull

out your watch with no kind of scruple. I have met with several instances of this in the course of my rambles ; but a day or two ago 1 found myself more than usually a subject of curiosity. I was alone in the street of embroidered handkerchiefs (every minute article has its peculiar bazaar), and wishing to look at some of uncommon beauty, 1 called one of the many Jews always near a stranger to turn a penny by interpreting for me, and was soon up to the elbows in goods that would tempt a female angel out of Paradise. As 1 was selecting one for a purchase, a woman plumped down upon the seat beside me, and fixed her great, black, unwinked eyes upon my face, while an Abyssinien slave and a white woman, both apparently her dependents, stood respectfully at her back. A small turquoise ring (the favorite colour of T urkev) first attracted her attention. She took up my hat, and turned it over in her soft, fat fingers, and dropped it again without saying a word. I looked at my interpreter, and he seemed to think it nothing extraordinary, and I went on with my bargain. Presently my fine-eyed friend pulled me by the sleeve, and, as I leaned towards her, rubbed her fore-finger very quickly over my cheek, looking at me intently all the while. I was a little disturbed with the lady's familiarity, and asked my Jew what she wanted. I found that my rubicund complexion was something uncommon among these dark skinned Orientals, and she wished to satisfy herself that I was not painted 1 I concluded my pur-

chase, and, putting the parcel into my pocket, did my prettiest at an Oriental salaam, but to iny mortification the lady gathered up her yashmack, and looked surprised out of her great eyes at my freedom. My Constantinople friends inform me that 1 am to lay no " unction to my soul" from her notice, such liberties being not at all particular. The husband exacts from his half-dozen wives only the concealment of their faces, and they have no other idea of inipiopriety in public. 'In the centre of the bazaar, occupying about as much space as the body of the City Ilall in New York is what is called the bczestein. You descend into it from four directions by massive gates, which are shut, and all persons excluded, except between seven and twelve in the forenoon. This is the core of Constantinople þÿ the soui and citadel of Orientalism. It is devoted to the sale of arms and costly articles only. The roof is loftier and the light more dim than in the outer bazaars, and the merchants who occupy its stalls are old and of established credit. Here are þÿ subjects for the pencil 1 If you can only take your eye from these Damascus sabres, with their jewelled hilts and costly scabbards, or from those gemmed daggers and guns inlaid with silver and gold, cast a glance along that dim avenue, and see what a range there is of glorious old gray-beards, with their snowy turbans ! These are the Turks of the old regime, before Sultan Mahmoud disfigured himself with a coat like a " dog of a Christian,'

and broke in upon the customs of the Orient. These are your opium-eaters, who smoke even in their sleep, and would not touch wine if it were handed to them by houris 1 These are your fatalists, who would scarce take the trouble to get out of the way of a lion, and who are as certain of the miracle of Mahomet's coffin as of the length of the pipe, or of the quality of the tobacco of Shiraz.' FIRST IMPRESSIONS OF LMlLAiSD. When 1 came on deck early on the 22d we had already left the North foreland and of Shoppy, with its wooded hills, Margate behind us ; on one side lay and the Island shortly after the somewhat lower coast of Essex came in sight. Vessels of every kind swarmed around us like sea-birds ; but when we reached Graverend, their number increased so much, and the beauty of the nearer and richly cultivated shores became so much greater, that I was involuntarily overcome by wonder and emotion. Recollections of the gradual upward course by which this happy island had for eighteen centuries been advancing to a pitch of elevation unmatched in the history of the þÿworld of the deeds and the sufferings, the exertions and the errors, the wars and the conquests, of her kings, her barrens, her churchmen, and her people þÿ all came crowding upon me. I enjoyed the delight of that high and generous enthusiasm which the ordinary incidents of life cannot call forth, and my whole journey seemed to me to be justified and rewarded by this single hour. But this was only rendered possible by my having been for years at home in England, and my having turned the strings of my head and heart for this jEolian touch of external impressions, by solitary historic labour. I was much moved by the sight of Tilbury Fort, where, in 1588, the high-hearted Elizabeth assembled and encouraged her troops, and thus caused the overthrow of Spain and a new organization of the world. From Tilbury to Woolwich the banks of

the Thames ape bare ; from Woolwich to Greenwich there are increasing signs of industry and cultivation ; until, on arriving at the Docks, you are borne along through absolute forest of ships. Compared with this, any thing of the kind that I have ever seen at Havre, Bordeaux, or Marseiles, is like a single room cut out of this immeasurable þÿpalace. It is true that here, as in Paris, the buildings are, at first sight, in no respect striking; but their very pecularities show a definite practical aim, which distinguishes them from ordinary buildings, and give them an interest of their own. If, however, the predominancy of mere utility and convenience, to the neglect of all considerations of beauty, be objected to English architecture, this crowd of ships is so far more striking and important a feature in the view, that all those of the land appear insignificant, Here one sees that London is the real capital of the world þÿ not Paris, in spite of the pretensions of its journalists and coteries. þÿ Paris is more perminently of the Town, Germany the Country, but London alone is entitled to talk of being the World. þÿ Raumer't England in 1835.

Scotch Songs. þÿ No man who lias lived among the peasanty of Scotland will deny the effects produced on them by their popular songs. During the expedition to Buenos Ayres a Highland soldier, while a prisoner in the hands of the Spaniards, having formed an attachment to a woman of the country and charmed by the easy life which the tropical fertility of the soil enabled the inhabitants to lead, had resolved to remain and settle in South Amerca. When he imparted this resolution to his comrade, the latter did not argue with him ; but leading liiin to his tent, he placed him by his side, and sung him " Lochaber no more." The spell was ori him. The tears came into his eyes, & wrapping his plaid around, him he murmured, " Lochaber nac mail ! þÿ 1 matin gang back þÿ Nal' The songs of his childhood were ringing in his ears, and he left that land of ease and plenty for the naked rocks and sterile valleys of Badcnoch, where at the close of a life of toil and hardship, he might lay his head in his mother's grave. þÿ Monthly Repository.

English Wealth. þÿ There was a countless train of equipages yesterday in Hyde Park ; the same in Regent's Park, and God knows where else ; and yet, on an average, no one keeps a carriage who has not 3000/. a year to spend. In comparison with the affluence which manifests itself here, the whole Continent seems poverty-stricken. Such wealth is very imposing, inasmuch as it is combined with so much industry, and is indeed chiefly its offspring. A combination of poverty and highmindedness may have a very good effect on l lie stage, but in every day life the union of affluence and high mindedness is far more " comfortable." þÿ Ilaumer's England in 1835.

W e are ever unwilling to circulate unpleasant intelligence, nor should we have now turned to the subject did not the prevalence of the epidemic make silence no longer a choice with us, in the discharge of our public duties. It is with unfeigned concern we now allude to the many deaths which have taken place within the last week or two in this community, and in such a manner as to warrant the only reasonable conclusion we can draw from the afflicting circumstance, that they have been occasioned by a fever, of what kind, but in spite of our continued exertions to learn, we have not yet been enabled to discover. There is one especial point, however insisted upon by the medical practioners of the town, and to which we must call the attention of every one þÿ that the epidemic is by no means dangerous, if proper medicines be administered to the patient upon the first symptoms of the attack. In most cases, therefore, where it has proved fatal, we infer that timely application must have been neglected, added perhaps to bodily predisposition to the disease. We hope this observation will meet the attention it deserves, and operate as a caution. The following remarks from the " Western Star" of yesterday arc also submitted, confident they will prove serviceable to all who may adopt them : " We should be remiss in our duty were we not to state that the epidemic which we slightly noticed in our last paper is now prevailing to an alarming extent. Numbers of valuable lives have within these few days been lost,
and many persons who arc now confined to their chambers, may be expected to pay the debt of nature. We do not wish to create alarm ; our aim is caution, and to recommend

©AW3IR T3S'X31TI>33X Bt'jS03a3S3W®3 ATltS. to every one a preparatory treatment, by an immediate attention to the state of the viscera. We shall not stop to inquire what the present fever may be denominated ; some say it is bilious, others say it is typhus ; and we rather agree with the latter þÿ it is sufficient to know that it is a malignant fever, widely spreading and mortal in its effects. We are no disci, pies of the Hygeists, but we are sufficiently liberal to do them every justice when we conscientiously think they merit it A little work was politely handed to us a day or two since, entitled " The Hygeian Treatment of the most prevalent diseases of the West Indies." It must be evident that Morison could not have produced from his own pen the many works of ability which are issued from the Hygeian College, nor can there be any doubt that he is assisted by medical men of eminence who have become converts to the Hygeian practice, lu page 73 of the work referred to, it is stated, and rationally so, that "in the common putrid or bilious lever (the corrupt matter still having its first scat in the prima vice, that is the stomach and intestines) chiefly fetid eructations, thirst, a bitter taste in the mouth, or like that of rotten eggs, vomitings, putrid stools, and worms, with an aversion to flesh, fish, and ail animal food, even to an egg it is also observed that, " with regard to the malignant fever, a sudden sinking of the pulse, prostration of strength, and lowness of spirits, a stinking breath, fetid evacuations of all kinds, so that even the smell of

the sweat and of the blood itself, are offensive, in an advanced stage of the disease. rl he tongue is black, deliriums, langours, and relaxations, eruptions and spots on the skin are frequent ; the urine, the excrements, and in extreme cases, the very sweats are bloody." " We have been led to say a few words upon the subject, in consequence of passing over in our minds the necessity of establishing a Medical Board, to be composed of gentlemen who have their diploma."., and other scientific men ot known skill and experience. This body should assemble at least once a week, and at times when any epidemic is prevailing, should report the state of heal th of persons in town and country They would also have the opportunity of mutually stating to each other the cases which have come under their hands, describe their treatment of their patients, and reciprocally make known to each other the success of their practice. " We respectfully call upon his honor the President to notice the foregoing remarks." We cannot but highly commend the suggestion of our cotern, with respect to establishing a Medical Board, if for 110 other reason than its proving satisfactory to most persons, to know whether the prevailing fever is upon the increase or not, by the report which it may be proper to issue at least once a week, of the state of health of the town. To the Police we would also sav a word upon the necessity of their keeping a watchful eye to the cleanliness of the streets and lanes

of the town, as it is well known that the most violent epidemics have either subsided or increased where this grand consideration has been made a lesser or greater object of public attention. 0 0 From the Dominica Observer, Aug. 10.
The Domestic Intelligence which we are called upon to announce this day is of the most painful kind and such as must constrain every lover of Dominica to acknowledge that

the Colony is about to sustain a public Bereavement unparralleled by any former one þÿ Our beloved Sir Evan Murray MacGrcgor is to leave us ! His Excellency has been appointed to the Government of Barbados and the Windward Islands, in the room of Sir Lionel Smith who is to assume the Governorship of Jamaica, vacant by the resignation of Lord Sligo þÿ Assailed by news so unexpected and in its results so lamentable to the interests of this devoted Colony, but just recovered from the baneful effects of political mis rule, the whole face of the Community (with one or two exceptions that we have heard of) has during the week been overcast with disappointment and grief. þÿ We can discourse together to no length, without giving vent to the absorbing thought þÿ " We are to lose our noble Governor!" And well may this be the case considering the revolting circumstances chilling to every lively thought, in which the people of Dominica were found at the time of the last arrival of Sir Evan amongst us þÿ Truly that w as a propitious season when from his exalted position the ken of the "Spirit of health" discovered our condition and forthw ith marked us lor renovation. A comparison of the actual state of society now existing, with that at the period to which we have referred must forcibly impress every unbiassed Observer with the important advantuger which under Divine Providence, our Governor General has conferred upon the Country. þÿ The path to Honour and Competency has, by him

been opened alike to all His Majesty's Subj cts without reference to their Colour or any other adventitious circumstances, however unfortunate these might have formerly been regarded, and to the period of latest posterity the pen of the Historian will have to register the acts of Governor MacGregor as those which had no precedent in Dominica þÿ amongst these will shine with prominent Splcnd ui the appointment of Justices of the Peace, without confinement to the Class from which alone such were selected even after that class had ceased to be the only legally privileged one. þÿ Saint Christopher Advertiser, Srpt ti.

RUSSIA. Private letters from St. Petcrsburgh in the Dutch papers contain the following, but we know that Lord Durham's representations arc treated in Russia with very little ceremonv: "At the instance of some English merchants, J.ord Durham, the British Ambassador, has complained of the obstructions thrown in the w ay of trade at the mouth of the Danube, and called the measures ordered on this subject presumptuous, and a violation of existing treaties. The measures in question have since been modified by the Russian government, and the obstacles complained of removed þÿ Whether it is owing or not to the complaints

of the English Ambassador is doubtful ; but it is said that in the answer to the British note, and especially with regard to the term presumptuous, it was observed on the part of Russia, that the policy of England in the East deserves the term presumptuous much more than that of Russia, its object being to obtain an influence in these countries dangerous to the interests of all other European þÿnations. In particular, notice is said to have been taken on this occasion, not only of the compelling of Mehemet Ali to give up his system of monopoly for the advantage of the British commerce, but also of the opening of a new channel of communication (on the Euphrates, by means of steam-boats) with the English possessions in India, through the centre of the Ottoman dominions ; which communication, in the opinion of Russia, is by no means intended to promote only the commercial interest of England, but also has political and military objects." þÿ London Standard, July 15.

The present position of Russia is of the utmost moment to Western Europe. She cannot remain stationary ; and it is impossible for her to move in any direction without carrying out her long-chcrished object of universal dominion. A war with Russia must be a defensive war on the part of Great Britain, Austria, and Erauce ; and in the event of such an occurrence, the first blow, if well directed, will be at least half the battle To suffer Russia to make herself mistress of Constantinople, would be to realize her own prediction in 1832 þÿ namely, to make no treaty with the English but at Calcutta. Three positions remain to be established þÿ firstly, that Russia cannot and will not remain content with her present conquests ; secondly, that her further acquisitions of territory must endanger the mercantile trade of England, and destroy the political influence of Austria and France ; and thirdly, that by a timely and judicious oombi nation on the part of these three Bowers, Russia will not only be compelled to retrace her devastating career in Ana, but even forced to restore the nationality of Roland. þÿ London Sun.

Though twenty years ago we paid Spain 600,000/. to relinquish the slave trade, and have a squadron on the African coast, to enforce the agreement, yet one man in Cadiz has forty ships afloat just now, all engaged in transporting slaves from the African coast to the island of Cuba, and the number of negroes imported into that Island last year (1835), exceeded '15,000. The Captain General ot Havannah takes a bribe of three guineas per head for every slave so imported, for conniving at the open transgression of 'his own public orders, proclaimed and placarded periodically, for no other purpose than to ridicule the English. The late increase in the value of sugar has given a great stimulus to the slave- trade. The Madrid Government could at any time put an cad to this nefarious trallic, if so disposed ; but it is notorious that they took the money with the full intention of not complying witli the treaty. So, at least, says the writer of a letter, dated Cadiz, June 20, 1830. þÿ Christian Advocate.

It is printed on two folio sheets, in Turkish and French; þÿ The latter is called the Moniteur Oriental. The one is read by the natives and raves, and the other by the Frank. It is issued with great exactness; and every Saturday morning it is sent up with our breakfast as regularly as a weekly paper in London. The Sultan takes great interest in it, reads it regularly, and is himself a contributer to it, writing sometimes the leading article. The contents of the paper are usually as follows : They commence þÿ with Constantinople and the concerns of the Turkish empire. The principal details are those of the army and navy, their movements and the change of officers, with bulletins of action by land or sea, fairly given, without much pompus Orientalism. Then follow civil affairs, events of the provinces, with always a favorable view of things, and an eulogium on the Sultan's measures for the good of the people. Then succeed news of other countries, with sometimes English Parliament, in which latter Mr. O'Connell cuts a conspicuous figure One could hardly imagine that violent democratic language would be permitted in a Turkish paper; as yet, however, it is harmless, for the people do not understand it. But the most extraordinary communication is a kind of budget, in which the receipts of public money are given, and the expenditure accounted for, with an accuracy of detail in piasters and paras, that would

please Mr. Hume. This is a thing before unheard of in Turkish policy ; where public money was a mystery, and every thing concerning it kept secret, both in its collections and expenditure. These subjects are varied with accounts of useful inventions, elementary sketches of the arts and sciences, and sometimes pleasing and instructive stories. þÿ The Turks, when this newspaper first appeared, had no conception of any amusement to be derived from such a thing; but, like children, when their curiosity was once excited) it knew no bounds. The publication of the news of the empire in this way soon became of universal attraction. The paper made its way to the coffee-houses, and the same Turk that I had noticed before dozing, half stupitied with coffee and tobacco, I now saw actually awake with the paper in his hand eagerly spelling out the news. But the most usual mode of communicating it arc news-rooms ; and a place is taken where those who wish to hear it assemble. A stool is placed in the centre, on which the man who can read sits, and others form a circle round him and listen. The attention paid is very different from that which 1 saw thein give to a storyteller. þÿ There was no mirth or laughter excited, but all seemed to listen with profound attention, interrupted only sometimes by a grave ejacu. lation of " Inshalish," "or Allah þÿKarim." which she receives another The first thing a Turk of any consequence is anxious to know is whether he has been mentioned, and what is said of him ; and in this

anecdote of the battle of new orleans. A daring Tennessean, with a blanket tied round him, and a bat, with a brim, of enormous breadth who seemed to be fighting ' on his own hook,' disdaining to raise his rifle over the bank of earth and fire in safety, to his person, like his more wary fellow soldiers, chose to spring, every time he fired, upon the breast-work, where, balancing, himself, he would bring his rifle to his cheek, throw back his broad rim, take sight and fire, while the enemy were advancing to the attack, as deliberately as though shooting at a herd of deer : then leaping down on the inner side, he would reload, mount the works, cock his beaver, take aim, and crack again. 4 Thus he did,' said an English officer who was taken piisoner by him, and who laughingly, related it as a good anecdote 4 five times in rapid succession, as I advanced at the head of my company ; and though the grape whistled through the air over our heads 1 could not help smiling at his grotesque, demi savage, demi quaker figure, as he threw back the broad flap of his casper to obtain a fair sight, deliberately raised his rifle ; shut his left eye, and blazed away at us. I verily believe lie brought down one of my men at every shot. As the British resolutely advanced, though our columns fell like the tall grain before the sickle at the fire of the Americans, the same officer, approached at the head of his bold granadiers, amid the rolling fire of musketry from the line of his unseen foes, undaunted and untouched. þÿ

44 Advance my men !' he shouted, as he reached the head of the foes þÿ ' follow me !' and, sword in hand, he leaped the dilch, and turning amidst the roar and flame of a hundred muskets to encourage his men, beheld to his surprise but a single man ol his company upon his feet þÿ more than fifty brave fellows, whom he had so gallantly lead on to the attack had been shot down. As he was about to leap back from his dangerous situation, his sword was shivered in his grasp by a rifle ball ; and at the same instant the daring Tennessean sprang upon the parapet, and levelled his deadly weapon at his breast, calmly observing. þÿ Surrender, stranger, or 1 may pcrlorate ye I' said the officer, at the close of his recilab 4 1 was compelled to deliver to the bold fellow my mutilated sword and pass over to the American lines þÿ The South West by a Yankee.

The 2nd August packet brings London dates to 15th ult. The affairs of Spain were in the most agitated and revolutionary state þÿ the Cities of Cadiz, Seville, Saragossa, Cordova, Malaga, Barcelona &c., trad declared for the constitution of 1812, þÿ and loudly insisted on a change of Ministry at Madrid, the National Guards had risen against the Military, hut had been put down by the latter under Quiroga the þÿ new Cortes has not yet assembled; the þÿ Queen regent had issued a Proclamation calling on all Spaniards to assist the Government in this emergency. Cordova is said to have resigned and General Saarsfield to he appointed in his place þÿ the National Guards at Madrid had been disbanded by the Queen. Spanish funds had fell in London to 32 pr. Ct. of their nominal value. In consequence of a body oi Carlists under Gomez having penetrated þÿCordova s lines and threatened Vigo, General Evans had detached part of his Legion to St. Andero, to endeavor to take the Carlists in the rear þÿ the Legion was in a mutinous state owing to not being paid. In England the differences between the Lords and Commons were as great as ever ; after long conferences by Committees ot hotli Houses, no settlement could he made of the Irish municipal and Tithes hills, which remained in Statu-Quo Mr. O'Connell had returned to Ireland ; þÿ declaring he had no hopes of Justice being done to his native country by the present Parliament. In France there were no indications of renewed disturbances þÿ the Ring of Naples had

arrived at Neuilly on a visit to Louis Philippe. The London papers announce the death of Rothschild, the great Banker ; he is said to have left Four millions Sterling his place þÿ will he tilled in the London house by his brother Charles Rothschild formerly of Naples, The decease of the celebrated Professor Schlcgcl is also announced at Copenhagen. At a late review of the Russian fleet at Cronstadt in com memoration of Peter the þÿGreat svisit to his ships, þÿ the Russian fleet extended six english miles, being composed of 25 Ships of the Line, (many of which are first rates,) 13 Frigates, besides Steamers and small vessels þÿ this is the largest Navy the Russians have ever collected, and well may excite the Jealousy of the neighboring powers.

By a late arrival from New York we have been favored with the papers of that city to 28th of August. President Jackson from his residence at the Hei milage in Tennessee, had written letters to the Governors of Kentucky and Tennessee, countermanding the requisition made upon them by Major General Gaines for one thousand men from each State ; The President censures General Gaines, and declares the intention of the Government of the 17. S. to preserve a strict neutrality in the contest between Mexico and Texas. Some extracts will he found below relative to that war; the Texian army are clamorous for the return of General Houston, to com mand them þÿ he was last recovering from his wound, and would immediately resume the the Mexican army under Urrea had its head quarters at Mctamoras, which had been declared in a state of Blockade by the Texians þÿ reports say the Mexicans were preparing to march into Texas in great force, hut volunteers continued to flock to the Texian

Standard, whose numbers had increased, in consequence of the countermanding orders of the President of the United States to the Kentucky arid Tennessee volunteers required hv General Gaines þÿ the latter, it is said, has not crossed the Sabine riverþÿ the Indian campaign in Florida w'ould he resumed in October þÿ that country being too sickly in the hot weather for white troops to campaign. þÿ

TEXAS. New Orleans, Aug. 11 þÿ Ry the arrival of the schr Fanny Butler, yesterday, in 4 days from Galveston, we have ascertained that no account had reached there (previous to the sailing the F.B.) of the prize said schooner been taken by the Texian armed of to have Brutus ; much less had her arrival been witnessed in the Bay ! The report originated with the officer who boarded the brig, in quest of provisions, and must have been made in bravado, as little or no specie has been shipped in Mexican vessels since the commencement of the Texian war. It appears that all the Mexican officers (prisoners) at Galveston, were about to be removed to Ana whan, on the Trinity ; the privates to remain at Galveston, General Goss is reported to have become quite a favorite with the army and people, being treated in the most courteous manner by both He states, in palliation of former conduct, that he was intent on keeping his promise inviolate, as lar as pledged ; hut that the Texians instead of guarding the Constitution of þÿ 24, and battling tor its privileges, declared an entire independence. This palliative seems to have its effect, judging from the the above. They also give him credit for humanity, in saving the lives of many, previous to the capture of Santa Anna. Matamoras, July 29. þÿ Dear Sir þÿ The army that retreated from Texas under the command of Filasola, is now at Matamoras, numbering 2309 ; and there has not been a Mexican soldier nearer Texas than the Brazos de Santiago, since their entrance into this

port. During a few days after their arrival they were in the most filthy state imaginable ; they 'might have been seen seated on the ground in groups, minutely surveying their calzoucillos and ridding themselves of those noxious animalcules, which are constant associates of tilth. Be it said to the credit of General Urrea, that the men are now in a good state of service, healthy and well clothed, and that good order and discipline arc maintained. It may he adduced as a proof of this, that, with one exception only foreigners have escaped being insulted ; this case was represented to Gen. Wool, who severely reprimanded ihe offender, in the presence of many of his fellow officers, and of the complainant. From the best information that I ean get, you may rest assured that the Mexicans will shortly enter on another campaign. There is no doubt but these troops will he reinforced by at least 4000, that a vessel is coming from Vera Cruz, with troops, provisions, and money, the whole of which will be put into operation ns quick as possible ; we learn nothing of this from the public prints, so that they are working secretly. I am of opinion that whenevef they may commence the campaign, it w ill be so directed that no one will have any preknowledge of their intention, and that "foreigners will he incapaciated to give any intelligence of their operations : this will be but reasonable policy, and what common prudence would dictate. The Texians must therefore, be on the alert

and unite, being convinced that if they gain their liberty, it must be by fighting and conquering again, and perhaps again ; and not by making treaties with/o isowers of War. Capts. Carnes and þÿ2 eale are yet in close prison, demonstrating the publicity of these people at d the credulity of the Texian Government. Don Francisco V. Fernandez, left this place for Victoria, on Monday last, --what he is about I know not.

Kentucky Volunteers Dibanded by order or General Jackson. þÿ The following letter addressed to Governor Morehead of Kentucky, was sent by an Express to Frankfort. General Combs, by order of the President, was the bearer of the news from the Hermitage. The letter was dated a fortnight since yesterday. Gen. Jackson to Governor Morehead. Sir þÿ Arriving at this place on the evening of the 5th instant, I was made acquainted w ith the requisition of Gen Caines on the Governors of Tennessee, Kentucky, Mississippi and Louisiana, for 1000 men from each State. The letter of Gen. Gaines and the proclamation of Governor Cannon, of Tennessee, made known the basis of this requisition Regarding the reasons assigned by General Gaines as not consistent with the relations which we have maintained with Mexico, since the existence of the civil war in Texas, or with those which it is our duty and wish to cultivate with that Government, as long as it observes good faith and friendship in its intercourse with the United States, I feel myself called on to inform you that that requisition has not received my approbation, and that I trust, if the men called for have been brought into the field, you will forthwith cause them to be mustered and discharged, and await lor further orders from the General Government in respect to any other requisition for the militia. The 10,000 volunteers authorizeded by the late act of Congress have been apportioned among the States and Territories nearest to the theatre of actual or apprehended hostilities

from the Indians. They are considered sufficient, combined with the regular troops, to maintain the peace of the frontier, and to terminate the war which now exists with the Creeks and Seminoles. All of them have not been brought into the field, but Gen. Gaines was notified that 1000 volunteers in Arkansas and 1000 in Missouri, had received orders to be organized and held in readiness for one þÿyear s ervice, should the emergency arise making their employment necessary on the frontier now commanded by him. This circumstance makes the present requisition of Gen. Gaines still more unaccountable particularly as it is believed that our Western frontier is now tranquil Under these circumstances, you will please cause the troops called for by the requisition in question, if
They will be paid as soon as an appropriation by Congress can be obtained for this purpose. 1 am, very respectfully, Your obedient servant. Andrew Jackson.

VERY LATE FROM TEXAS. Nacogdoches, July 25. þÿ We have just heard from the army. They arc yet at Victoria, the number about 2,300. Lamar, who was appointed Major General by the cabinet, went on to assume the command, and on his arrival was informed by the army that they would not obey any order from him, or from the cabinet, unless it came through the proper channel þÿ nor would they recognize any commander in-chief except General Samuel Houston. This intelligence is brought here by two men just from the army þÿ and I have no doubt is true. The army decided by a vote of more than 1,700 to 170. I left Gen. Houston yesterday. His wound is rapidly recovering,

LaTe from Texas. þÿ A slip from the Natchez Free Trader (Aug. 0.) contains a letter from a gentleman just arrived from Texas, which confirms the intelligence previously received of the arrival of Gen. Gaines at Nacodoches, with four companies of U. S. troops, and six companies of infantry. Bowles, the Cherokee Chief, whose hostility to the U. States, we announced some days since, this letter says, now calls himself a Mexican Colonel. The Texian and Mexican army are about 300 miles distant. Gen. Lamar has sent two companies to bring Santa Anna to his headquarters. Gen. Houston, it the letter can be credited, is opposed to inflicting any þÿ violence upon Santa Anna. Gen. þÿHouston s health is improving.

From Mexico and Texas we have later news. Many of the Texan prisoners have been liberated, and among them, captains Carnes and Miller. These prisoners were taken at Metamoras in a most vile, treacherous, Mexican-like manner. The prisoners, immediately after being set free, marched for the Colorado, there again to join the Texian army. Captain Teal was still kept a prisoner, and one of his companions (Capt Carnes) refused to leave Metamoras without him. The cholera is committing great ravages in the Mexican army, and has driven it buck to Metamoras.
It is calculated, and is probably true, that 15000 persons arrive in this city every day, and that as many or nearly as many leave the city.

(From the St. Thomas Times, Sept. 21, 1830.) In our columns of to-day, will be found an article extracted from the Barbados, New Times, þÿ we wmuld strictly recommend it to the attention of our readers, as it may be an interesting piece of information to the public in general. There will be seen the defects that is likely to arise from the þÿ Colonial Bank" that may be established in this place as well as in all the other Colonies, in a very short time. We published sometime ago, a Jamaica Prospectus for a Bank to be established in that Island, to be conducted on its own Colonial footing þÿ the prospects of which seems to be very promising for the general good. The prospectus that is now published in Demerara for a Bank with a capital of £300,000, will also show, that the prospects of the þÿ Colonial þÿBank cannot prove any way satisfactory to the Colonists ; in the article, will also be found strong recommendations to the Barbados people, to try and establish a Bank on its own island principles. We cannot but believe now, after seeing the exertions made by the most valuable of the Colonies in endeavouring to establish Banks on their own footing, that the said þÿ ColonialBank" wall prove highly injurious to the prospects of the Colonies generally. We would ask, why the People of this place do not try and form such an establishment 1 we are quite sure there are funds sulheient for so doing.

From the Barbados þÿ New Times." We have observed, in late Demerara papers, that the Prospectus of a Bank on really Colonial principles, has just been submitted to that Colony by a Mr. Robertson ; a gentleman, we understand, highly qualified by knowledge and business habits for this undertaking. Our opinion as regards the miscalled þÿ Colonial þÿBank projected by Messrs. Irving and Co., has now been sometime before the public. The three capital defects of this scheme were, in our opinion þÿ first, the insignificantly small number of shares reserved for residents in the Colonies: secondly, the therefore exclusive a is þÿi Colonial management of its operations! and thirdly, the invidious prohibition to lend on fixed securities. The prosperity of these Colonics evidently depends on the prosperity of their agricultural interest ; and this prohibition clashing, as it obviously docs, with that interest, was itself a sufficient objection to the

scheme. But how infinitely was this objection cncreased in force by the undisguised fact, that in reserving to the resident Colonies only one seventh of the shares þÿ and in seating the government of the Bank in London instead of the Colonies þÿ the projectors of the scheme had entirely excluded the resident planters þÿ the real agricultural interest of these Colonies þÿ from any participation in the management of those operations from any þÿ controul over those commercial speculations which, þÿ carried beyond a certain point, might totally ruin them ! There is certainly some truth in the observation that we here take the worst possible view of the case. No prudent man, however, will censure us for erring on the side of prudence. In a case of so vital importance, we should not be contented to guard against probabilities only, þÿ we should tase into consideration and, as far as wo arc able, provide against possibilities as well. It is possible that any Bank under the most judicious management may fail þÿ but we cei tainiy render this possibility more remote by lacing the management under the immediate c< ntroul of those whom its failure will most injure þÿ whose stake in the concern bears the greatest proportion to the apparent profit hcio out by any doubtful speculation ; and who e, therefore, least likely to engage in such speculation 1 These were the groundsel oar opposition to the Colonial Bank. As we stated from the first, we are clearly opinion, of as far as our knowledge goes, that a Bank on
proper principles would be really beneficial to these Colonies ; and we are happy to see that such a Bank is likely to be established in British Guiana.

Local Banks, it would appear, are the order of the day. In Demerara the Prospectus of the British Guiana Banking Company has been published, the shares in which are to bo cunfined to residents of the Colony, and in Barbados it is proposed to have a similar establishment. Whether these will be broi c oc.o operation before the Colossus puts th its mighty branches in those islands, we are not prepared to say.þÿ Jamaica Watchman.

A QrEF.it Article of Commerce. þÿ May Bros, we are informed, are becoming a new article of commercial enterprise. A society formed for the purpose, nt Guedelinbourg, lias caught 19,000,000 of May Bugs to make oil of them. They have already made the attempt in Hungary, and obtained three measures of oil, from eight measures of the May Bug. They put the insects into earthen pots covered with straw or a tissue of metalic threads, and turn them over upon a heated vessel, which is destine to receive the oil which flows out þÿ this oil is particularly good for greasing wheels.

Narrow Escape. þÿ An Irish laborer þÿ one who labored under the inconvenience of being unable to walk in a straight line þÿ on Sunday morning last, toppled off the high banks, a few r ids below the Falls on the Canada side, and fell forty or fifty feet upon a projecting rock, which saved him from the yawning gulph beneath. The roar of the water drowning his cries for assistance, he was not discovered until several hours after his fall, when he was picked up with some of his limbs broken, and his body otherwise severely bruised. He is doing well, and is likely to recover from his injuries. þÿ Nigara Paper.

A Portable fire escape Ladder has been constructed, says a foreign paper, which three men in the space of halt a minute can raise to the top of a three story building. It is constructed on the principle of military scaling ladders, but much lighter, and in short lengths of about six feet. The top joint is equipped with a pair of small wheels in order to clear all projections and facilitates its traversing up the wall ; an axle and universal pulley with a belt and rope, is also attached to this point for the jiurposc of lowering females and infirm poisons.

TEXAS. The prospect of the independence of Texas has given rise to some extraordinary projects and speculations among the citizens of the United States. Among them is a truly magnificent one started in New Orleans, which, if carried into effect, will create a new era in the commercial operations of that part of the Union. It is well known that steam boats of 500 or 600 tons burden can ascend the Red River as high as Nachitoohes, and it is now proposed that a railroad should be construe;- d from that point, through a gorge in the Southern Rocky Mountains, and thence to the Gulf of California. Such a work would give to New Orleans, on access to the trade of the East Indies, China, Japan, and the coasts of the Pacific, which would set competition at defiance. The route to India and the western coast of South America would in fact, be shortened more than onc-half. þÿ Times.

From the Barbadian, September 17. We had not room on Wednesday to finish oui summary of the Packet intelligence. It is now resumed. The accounts from that distracted country, Spain, increase in interest. Insurrectionary movements had taken place in many of the principal towns against the Government of the Queen, who it was supposed would be compelled to adopt the Constitution of 1812. In our last we published an analysis of this free Constitution from the John Bull. The Q þÿueen s cause was certainly on the wane, while her enterprising opponent, Don Caklos, or Charles the 5th, as the Tory papers call him, was rising in splendour. His influence and power were extending þÿ his arms were victorious, while the British Legion, disconcerted and discontented, and in want of money, exhibited strong symptoms of decay and dissolution. In short, they were in a state of actual mutiny. This civil war, which is draining the kingdom of Spain of its blood and treasure, and has been carried on in a merciless and sanguinary spirit, is, shame to our liberal Government, kept up by the tortuous policy of England. Professing non intervention, the British Ministers send ships, and men, and money, and arms, to assist a Queen de facto , against a King de jure, as Tory politicians will have it.

The Imperial Parliament, it was conjectured, would be prorogued about the 18th of August. Mr. þÿO Connell has been so exceedingly kind and considerate as to postpone, until next session, his intended motion to reform the House of Lords, by introducing the elective principle, and thereby making it a Representative assembly, 658 K presentatives in the House of Commons not being sufficient, in the Agitator's opinion, for his revolutionary scheme. It is our opinion, that the hereditary branch of the Legislature stands in higher estimation than ever with the people þÿ not the þÿpopulace for we apprehend there is a wide difference between th q populace and the people. When we speak of the people, we mean the great bulk of the nation þÿ when we speak of the populace, we mean the mere multitude the vulgar, the rabble, or, as the French say, the canaille.

The Examiner of Sunday called Lord Clanricarde a rising man. Lord Clanricarde was determined to justify the opinion of the Examiner, and on Tuesday went up in a balloon. On the same day, Captain Curry ascended, for the second time, with Mrs. Graham, from þÿSadler W s ells. They were in the clouds for an hour and a half. Mrs. þÿGraham s letters on aerostation are extremely satisfactory; she deprecates the idea of danger þÿ tells us how well, upon another occasion, a naval gentleman managed his grappling irons, and she was, contrary to her own desire of soaring, þÿ obliged to check the ascending power of the machine, in order that her companion might have a good view of the þÿcountry. Upon the delights of the ascent of Tuesday Mrs. Graham has written a letter, which we find in Friday's Times, and certainly it sounds exceedingly tempting. The fair voyager says þÿ after they had passed immediately over the Imperial Gas Company's works, at H aggerstone, they obtained an altitude of 15,950 feet. þÿ Captain þÿCurrie, says Mrs Graham in her letter, was so delighted, that in a moment of þÿ extasy suddenly he exclaimed. How awfully beautiful, how enchanting, oh, Mrs. Graham! we will never return to the earth þÿagain. The Captain, continues Mrs. Graham in her letter, þÿ at this time made a slight experiment with a small aparatus, which convinced him of the correctness of Mrs. þÿGraham assertion, s that he was competent to undertake and complete the task of steering a machine of any

dimensions, where he þÿpleases. Now, if this desideratum can be really obtained, and balloons he directed and guided to given points, the discovery may be rendered as useful as it is now beautiful. Even as it is, to what a taste of ease and comfort these journeys or voyages are now reduced! When Mr. Harris, some years since, took up a Miss Stocks with him, it was remarked Stocks never rose so rapidly before. Mr Harris, however, when be was up, gave

Miss Stocks the valve line to hold, while he was employed about something else. Miss Stocks pulled hard, the valve opened, the gas escaped, down came the Machine, and Mr. Harris was unfortunately killed. Miss Stocks was slightly hurt, and went up with another gentleman the week after. On Tuesday the Greens go up again from Vauxhall, and a magnificent sight it is to see; a ship launch is finer only because when the vast body glides away and leaves the spectators looking at each other as people at dinner would look if the table were suddenly to sink through the floor, a thousand associations are conjured up in the mind þÿ the uses, the destinies, the glories which await her, the services she is to do, the triumphs she is to þÿachieve these are undefmable ; but the soaring of a balloon from your þÿfoot the uprising of the people with whom you have just shaken hands, is glorious to þÿsee -and if man have a feeling in heart worth caring for, he will find it oosing out of the corner of his eye. The only drawback is the evident inutility of the success of the discovery, and Mr Green, who is decidedly hitherto a great master of his art, has more satisfactorily, or perhaps we should say unsatisfactorily, than any body else, proved thi3 inutility by his late experiments with two balloons I he tall, flat-hatted, good looking man who rejoices in the name of Lennox, and who, having come over last year from France in a steam-boat, bringing with him his aerial ship, which he said could come or go as he pleased,

grounded his theory of the possibility of directing balloons upon the existence of varying currents at different degrees of altitude, so that by managing most ingeniously his descent or ascent, by means of an addition or reduction of atmospheric air In an interior balloon, be could always find a fair wind Mr. Green, by pairing oft; has shown the futility of this principle; his balloons at higher, or lower, or equal elevations, took the same course, one going perhaps faster or higher, but still in the some direction, as well as a pilot which kept with them last Tuesday as long as we could see. Mr. Buxton, whose remark to Mr. Attwood on the þÿ Bunch of þÿGreens we noticed last week, was very much struck by Mr þÿGreen s own observations upon the establishment of this fact, ami made a sort of supplementary addition to Ins previous bit of facetiousness; for, upon seeing his friend, on Thursday, after þÿ having read Mr þÿGreen s opinion as to the he drift of the þÿair, he told him that, had seen the bunch of Greens in tiie although clouds, it was evident there was no currents there. Now, from what Mrs. Graham says, it appears that her husband is even yet confident of success. We wish he may reap the laurels he well deserves it he achieves his object.

A physician, in Prussia, lately prescribed a medicine powder to the wife of a stock-broker, in the quantity of the doses of which it was necessary to be very precise, and therefore, directed that they should be equal to the weight of a ducat. The physician on calling on the following day found his patient's malady increased to an alarming degree. He earnestly inquired whether the medicine had been administered. The husband answered in the affirmative, and as a proof, produced the empty box. " Good God 1" exclaimed the physician, " How is this? The quantity I directed to be given was not more than a tweitli !" " Oil !" replied the man of money, " not having a ducat in the house, 1 took three Prussian crowns, which are equal to a ducat, and even took care to add the agio, according to the last quotation at the exchange !"

SKETCHES OF THE LIFE OF JOHN PAUL JONES. A life of the celebrated John I'aul Jones was published a few years since in the United States, and it is full of interest to naval amateurs ; his original name was John Paul, and the place of his birth near Dumfries, in Scotland, he was born in 1 747 ; at the early age ol thirteen he espoused with ardour the cause of liberty and independence, in the struggle which ensued between America, and the Mother country; he had a brother much older than himself, who had settled in Virginia and who had acquired some property there, which lie bequeathed to his favourite brother John ; tilts was the first cause of his emigration to America. Our Hero, who had previously commanded Ships in the British merchant service, trading with the West Indies, on the breaking out of the war between Great Britain, and her Cidevant Colonies in 1775, obtained the appointment of Lieutenant in the U. S. Navy; he was the first man who hoisted the flag of the new born nation, on Ship board, in the year 1776, in the liver Delaware. Jones soon after his appointment, obtained the command of the Sloop of War Ranger of IS Guns, with the rank of Post Captain, and, as many excesses, but ning oj towns, &c., had been committed by British men of war, on the American coast, and as many Americans had been carried, to England and treated in the most cruel and rigourous manner ; þÿ Jones, whose whole heart and soul were engaged in the cause of his adopted country, suggested to Congress, the propriety of retaliating for these

wanton cruelties, bv a cruise on the coast of Great Britain, and by making them feel at home, some of the evils, they were inflicting upon their refractory colonies. Accordingly Jones received orders to pro. ceed to Europe ; he arrived safe in France, and he soon after sailed on a cruise in the British channel, (having previously rendered most important services to his adopted country by the capture of a great part of the clothing and supplies destined for the army of General Burgoyne, but which by this capture were opportunely transferred, to that of the great Washington) He cruised in the Irish Channel ; landed in Scotland ; spiked the Guns> and took possession of Forts ; destroyed many merchantmen, and spread terror and dismay throughout Great Britain ; þÿ he continued to cruise off their const, and espied the British Sloop of War Drake, lying at anchor in the harbour of Cari ickfergus ; Jones lay too for her; she came out to give him battle; and after a well fought action of one hour, the Drake, struck her flag to the Star-Spangled banner þÿ1 Jones returned safe to France with several prizes, <Sc by the assistance of his friend Dr. Franklin, (plenipotentiary of the U. S to the court of France,) Jones fitted out a Squadron; having obtained a large East-Indiaman for his flagship, which incomplimcnt to Franklin he named uthe Rnnhomme Richard" She was a fast sailer & Frigate built and mounted 4(lgtins þÿ in company with the American Frigate Alliance, (commanded by Landais, a French Officer) and of two or three

smaller v essels ; Jones sailed again, on a cruise in the channel ; and off Ffamboro head, he fell in with a large convoy of merchant vessels, tinder convoy of the fine new Frigate Serapis of 44 Guns, and the Countess of Scarborough sloop of war of 24 Guns. On sight of Jones' squadron signals were made by the
Serapis for the convoy to disperse ; the Frigate standing a different course, and the

Jones, solely intent on glory gave chase to the Serapis, (regardless of the convoy.) The superior sailing of the Bon homme- Richard enabled hei to come up with the Serapis, who was making for England ; Jones having left his own squadron out of sight, when night come on ; þÿ but it was full moon and about 8 o'clock in the evening Jones in attempting to cut ofl the Serapis from the land intentionally run on board of that Frigate, her bowsprit crossing his miseumast, and Jones with his own hands lushing the two ships together with the ropes hanging from the bowsprit of the Serapis. A most deadly combat ensued, the Guns of the two ships nearly touched each other. The superior metal of the Serapis, (long 18S) completely riddled the Bonnehomme Richard, whose largest cannon were long nines and twelves ; both ships were repeatedly on fire, the lower deck Guns of the Bonnehouune Richard were all silenced, but Jones was on the quarter deek,& directed the cannon loaded with double headed shot, at the mainmast ot the Serapis, which he shot away ; after a most furious ba.tle ol two hours, the Alliance came up, and raked both ships as they lay lushed together, and at ten o'clock the Serapis struck her flag, having nearly one hundred men kilted, and the Bon-hoirime- Richard as many, the Countess of Scarboro soon after struck her flag. The Bonnehomme Richard sunk shortly after the baitlc ; Capt. Jones having scarcely time to remove his crew to the Serapis; much blame was attached to Landais by Jones for

firing into both ships, and not eoming up soon, cr the former was afterwards broke. Jones got safely into the Texel with his prizes and nearly 600 prisoners ; all England was alarmed, þÿ Forty sail ol men of war were cruising after him, around Great Britain, and a fleet was sent to the Texel to watch his motions ; notwithstanding which, his great knowledge of tlie coasts of the channel enabled him to evade them all and to carry the Serapis safely into b ranee, he also succeeded in an object dear to bis heart, in having his prisoners exchanged for Americans detained in England. Jones was received with acclamation in France; þÿ Louis 16th conlercd upon him the military order of merit, (at that time rarely given to foreigners) ; he also received the rank of Chevalier, and an elegant gold hilled sword from the King with a most flattering motto inscribed upon it. Jones soon alter returned to the United States in the Ariel sloop of war. þÿ Landuis, in the frigate Alliance having precceded him, (running away from France with that ship, altho' ordered by the American Minister Dr. b ranklin, to give her up to Jones), Jones on his passage home fell in with a British 20 Gun ship which after aa action of 10 or 15 minutes si ruck her flag to him, hut she being a superior sailer, when he was preparing to take possession of her, filled her sails, and got ofl' it being a dark night. Capt. Jones was well received by Congress who passed a most flattering vote of thanks for lus services, with the presentation of a

superb sword, the rank of first post Captain, or senior Oj/icer oj the Navy, and they ordered a 74 Gun ship called "the America" to be built for him, and gave him the superintendance of her equipment, Landais was tried and dismissed the navy, but was saved from

further punishment, by the plea of insanity being successfully made for him. sloop of war following the same example þÿ When the America was getting ready for launching, the French Fleet then at Boston, lost one of their 74's called " the Magnifigue," by the carelessness of the American Pilot ; and Congress resolved to offer the America as a present to the French Admiral the Marquis de Vaudrueil, to make up for the loss ; this was a great disappointment to Captain Jones, but at the request of Admiral de Vaudrueil, Captain Jones was invited to accompany him to the West Indies in his own flag Ship, for the mutual instruction of both in Naval tactics, Jones was treated with great attention on board the fleet and his opinion often followed, in their course, nearly 60 officers of Count Rochambeau's army were on board the flag Ship, and Jones became acquainted wi h many of high rank and merit, they arrived at St. Domingo, and had the war continued, they were to have attempted the conquest of Jamaica ; but news of peace arrived soon after, and Jones had the satisfaction to hear on board the fleet the official announcement of the acknowledgment of the Independence of his adopted country, as a free Sovereign, and Independent nation ! he returned to the U. S., and was soon after intrusted by Congress with a mission to b ranee to settle and adjust claims growing out of the war as regarded prize money due to him and to his Squadron ; he succeeded in obtaining payment after a delay of two years, and having no further employ in

the United States, and weary of inactive life, Jones, after a prolonged stay at Paris, in the year 1787, at the earnest solicitation of the Russian Ambassador at Paris, and by command of his Sovereign, offered Jones high rank in the Russian Navy; þÿ In consequence, he proceeded to St. Petersburg where he was most graciously received hy the Empress Catherine, and hy Prince Potemkin, and war being about to take place with the Turks, the rank and pay of Rear- Admiral and the command of a fleet in the Black Sea, were conferred upon him, whose equipment he superintended ; at that time the Turks were greatly superior in Naval power in the Black Sea. to the Russians, and the Captain Pasha block aded them at the entrance of the river I.iman ; but Jones repeatedly foiled him in every attempt to attack him, took several of his Ships, and hy his judicious measures materially eontributed to the success of the famous campaign of 1788, in which the armies ol Potemkin and Surwarrow so greatly distinguished themselves; but Admiral Jones had united with him in his naval command, the Prince of Nassau; a French naval officer in the service of Russia, who envying Jones' superior talents and courage, took a great dislike to him, which he also infused into Potemkin, with whom Nassau was a great favorite ; and Potemkin had Jones recalled to St Petersburg, where he soon after left the Russian service in disgust, having previou9|y received the military order of St Anne, and flattering

compliments from the Empress Catherine. Jones returned to Paris where he remaincd 'till the year 1792, and lie died there in the summer of that year, the National assembly having ordered a deputation of twelve of their members to attend his funeral and appointed an orator to deliver a funeral eulogy over his body, altho' hut of middle age he was worn out with the fatigues of over exertion in his profession. A commission had been sent to him from the United States to treat with Algiers and

the Barbary powers, and to conclude a peace with them, but it arrived at Paris alter his death. Adirrral Jones during his life, enjoyed the confidence and friendship of Franklin, Washington, La Fayette, Itochambeau, Counts lVEstning, de Vergennes, l)e Segur, De Vnudrueil, D'Orvillinrs, and many others. The virtuous and unfortunate Louis 16th was very friendly to him, and beguiled some of the weary hours of his imprisonment in the temple, in perusing a Journal of Jones' naval life prepared expressly for that Monarch, by Jones himself. On visiting Copenhagen in 1787 he had the honor of dining with the King of Denmark who conferted a pension upon him ; he also enjoyed the favor of a long and confidential interview with the crown prince. þÿ Jones left some property which he bequeathed to his sisters, Mrs. Taylor, and Mrs. Loudon of Dumfries, Scotland, with whom he always kept up a friendly correspondence ; he was never married, altho' a favorite with some of the first Ladies at Paris ; he had considerable talents as a poet, and many of the effusions of his muse were dedicated to the fair of his acquaintance ; he wrote well in prose, and his life contains numerous memorials and letters written in a clear, and nervous style ; he had many rival jealousies to contend with during his life, owing to his being a foreigner in the different services he entered ; but his perseverance was great, and a love of glory, united with a strong attachment to his adopted country, were the impelling motives of his actions. þÿ
