This is a species of action which, in our opinion, reflects disgrace upon the boasted civilisation of England. The action to recover compensation in damages is founded upon the priuciple that the dishonor of a wife is a trespass upon the property of the husband, and like a trespass on other property, to he compensated bv money Can any thing be more gross, more truly barbarous, we may say, than this notion of a pecuniary compensation for such an injury ? How can persons, moving in a sphere of life where one expects to meet with nice feelings of honor, and some degree of elevation of sentiment reconeil it to their notions of proprietory, to come into a court of law to ask compensation in money for an injury which if rightly felt, can admit of no compensation ? If among those who move in the higher walks of life " the sensibility of honour which feels a stain as a wound," were more prevalent than it is, we should never hear of actions of this sort at least among thaj class of society. Public morals would he better protected by the concealment than the exposure of those things, which till the journals with what ofiends good taste, pollutes the young mind, impairs the delicacy of the females character, and ministers to a depraved curiosity among all classes of people. In other countries we hear of no such actions. If the legislature look as much rare of public morals in this country as of public health, it would be no less penal for any parties to spread the moral contagion of such
actions throughout the land, than to wilfully contaminate the physical health of the people with the intcction of the plague. þÿ Herald.
He that sins against men may fear discovery, but he who sins against Cod is sure ol' it. þÿ Jones of Nay land.

Oukasmaim. Sin Alexander Bali, was one of those I great men who adorned our navy at the end | of the last century. Though less known, per- i haps, to the present generation than seveial of bis contemporaries, he was inferior to none of them ; and, in many respects it would be difficult to name his equal. To bravery, decision, and energy, he added a sound judgment, a meditative mind, and the most unwearied benevolence. The following anecdotes are from the pen of his friend, the poet Coleridge, in a larire party at the Grand Master's Palace in Malta, 1 had observed a naval officer, of distinguished merit, listening to Sir A. Ball whenever he joined in the conversation, with a mixed expression of awe ami atlbction, that gave a more than common interest to so manly a countenance This officer afterv Is told me that he considered himself indented to Sir Alexander for that which was dearer to him than his life. " When he was I .ieut. II ill," said he, he was the officer I accompanied in my first boat-expedition, being then a midshipman, and only in my fourteenth year. As we were rowing up to the vessel which we were to attack, amid a discharge of musketry, 1 wa3 overpowered by fear, and seemed on ihe point of fainting away, Lieutenant Bail, who saw the condition 1 was in, placed himself close beside me, arid still keeping his countenance, directed towards the enemy pressed my hand in the most friendly manner, and said in a low voice, ' Courage, my dear boy, you will recover in a minute or so ; 1 was just the same

when I first went out in this was ' " Sir," added the officer to me, " it was as if an an go| had put a new soul into mc. With the feeling that I was not yet dishonoured, the whole burden of agony was removed ; and, from that moment. I wa ss a fearless & forward as the oldest of the boat's crew."

For some time a coldness existed between Lord (then Captain) Nelson and Captain Ball. When both their ships were together close off Minorca, Nelson's vessel was nearly disabled by a violent storm, and Captain Ball took it in tow. and used his best endeavours to bring her into Port Mahon. Nelson, believing that boih ships would be lost, requested Captain Ball to let him loose, and on his refusal became impetuous, and enforced his demand with passion" ate threats. Captain Ball then took a speaking-trumpet and calmly replied, " 1 feel confident that I can bring you in safe ; I, therefore, must not. arid, by the help of Almighty God, I will not, leave you!" What he promised he performed ; and after they were safely anchored, Nelson came on board of Ball's ship, and embracing him with all the ardour of acknowledgment, exclaimed " A friend in need is a friend indeed." This was the « ginning of a firm and perfect friendship between these two great men. þÿ Coleridge's Friend.

A long life may be passed without finding a friend in whose understanding and virtue we can equally confide and whose opinion we can value at once for its justness and sincerity. A weak man, however honest, is not qualified to judge. A man of the world, however, penetrating, is not tit to counsel. Friends are often chosen for similitude of manners. and therefore each palliates the other's failings because they are his own. Friends are tender and unwilling to give pain; or tney are interested, and fearful to offend þÿ Johnson.

How a Man Married his own Sister. þÿ The Dedham Patriot says that a marriage once took place at Canton, Massachusetts, under the following circumstances. The bridegroom when quite a small boy, ran away from his parents who lived in Lower Canada. In process of time, the father died the mother þÿ married again, and the fruits of this union were several daughters. The daughter grew up and the parents not having the means to support them, they went to work in factories. One strayed to Canton factory, where by a fortuitous circumstances, the runaway happened to be at work. He soon became acquainted with this girl, and before a full his. tory of each other's origin was developed, married her In a few days it was ascertained tlrat they both had one mother This (f course greatly confused and astonished both parties, from which arose strong conscientious scruples as to the propriety of brother and sister living together in a state of matrimony ; and upon mature consideration they resolved mutually to dissolve their connexion as man and wile.

Maketh Known: Whereas by the manumission ol Slaves in these colonies, either by purchase or deeds of gift, several ill usages have gradually crept in. and are daily in. creasing, whereby not only the spirit and intentions of those principles, which of late have been adopted with regard to the facili. tating and promoting manumissions, are misconstrued ; but opportunities are given to selfinterested speculators, heedless of the consequences, with fair promises to misguide those, whose protection always has been an object of paternal care of our most gracious King ; and as also infringement on the rights of private individuals, and Evasion of the existing laws against the exportation of Slaves from His Majesty's Golonies, may with reason be apprehended from the frequent and hasty manumissions, either by purchase or deeds ol gilt, which of late have taken place, 1 have deemed it necessary, to guard against these evils, and for the due preservation of good order and the right of property to stipulate as an Ordinance for these Colonies, as I do hereby stipulate and command : That persons whom hereafter obtain their freedom bv purchase, deeds of gift or in any other manner, will not be allowed in the first 12 Months from the recording of such manumission, to leave His Majesty's Colonies, unless being provided with a special permission tor that purpose trom the Government concerned, without which no passport must be given. Those that assist such persons in leaving the Colonies without passport as well as Mas-

ters ol Vessels carrying them away, will be punished in analogy with the stipulations of the Roval Ordinance of 1st June 1832, concerning the punishment, of those, that forward the absconding of Slaves from the Danish Westindia Islands.

from tiie portsmouth journal. THE ART OF M 1 KINO MONEY PLENTY IN EVERY MAN'S POCKET. Dr. Franklin undertook to teach his countrymen this art, many years ago; and if they had followed his prescriptions in relation to this important matter, we should at this time all ot us be þÿ not perhaps rich, þÿ but extremely comfortable. His rule was simply this, " spend every day one penny less than thy clear gains." So sim pie and plain that the people despised it, and have ever since been listening to quack doctors, who pretended to know more about political economy than Dr. Franklin, or than even Solomon himself, from whose book Franklin borrowed a number of It avrs. A few years ago, mechanics' wages were low here, and few employed, at some trades. One of the quacks told us. that if we would put down the aristocracy, by which he meant to put himself into ollice work would þÿ be plentiful, wages high, lie was put in þÿ did not seem to make much difference the þÿ but it world went on very much as it had done ; he grew richer, to be sure ; but the mechanic was as poor as ever. The farmers were told, much about the same time, by another quack doctor, that produce was very cheap, because the British West India ports were closed, þÿ and that pork would certainly rise when they were opened The ports were opened, and the pork did rise- 44 We told you so," says the quack ; as if the opening of the ports were the cause, w hen it was well known that no pork went to those ports ; þÿ and it was moreover, matter of com-

mon lame that the rise of pork w as caused bv the State of New Hampshire "going the whole hog" for Jackson. Money would be plentter it the banks would discount, says one : þÿ the banks would discount if money were plentier, sajs another: both probably correct ; each looking at one side of the case only. One set of quack doctors (not Botanic, but Mineral.) proposed to make money plentier by coining gold pieces, þÿ but they were too heavy for circulation, though they may have been useful in another way, for the sight of them is said to be good for sore eyes. Another, or some of the same, told us that every thing would go on smoothly in the money market, if we would only dispense with small hills, which were declared to be a nuisance and a trouble, and withal highly aristocratic and dangerous. The small bills become rather scarce, and now a poor housekeeper can hardly open his mouth short of a five dollar bill, or keep thanksgiving without getting a note discounted at the Bank. All this will do pretty well for the farmers, that independent yeomanry of which we have heard a good deal, þÿ but it comes rather hard upon us poor citizens, when wc have to work for our old wages, and pay double price for every thing we eat. þÿ Can't you convince them that we don't get a five dollar bill for a day's work, though small change is out of the question ? If you can, although you may not make money plenty in all pockets, you may at least put bread in every house. And can't you also show the people, that

the plenty or scarcity of money cannot much disturb those persons who are not in debt ? If you can, and make them believe it, they will find, that he who never gets trusted, need not fear hard times. So says PoOR ltlCHAKO.

Newport, Isle of Wight, Oct. 11. þÿ The Southern coast of this island is now the scene of a shipwreck more dreadful in its effects than any which has occurred on these shores for many years past. The ship (Jiaredon, of Loudon a 10 tons burthen, Samuel Walkers master, bound from St Christopher's to London with a cargo of rum, sugar and cocoanuts, was this morning, about half past live, stran ded at Black Caug Chine, and within an hour of her striking, not two timbers remained together. The whole of her passengers and crew, twenty-eight in number, with the exception of three, have met a watery grave, and owing to the tremendous sea running at the time, a verj small portion ot the cargo is saved. The survivors are James Harris, second mate; Win. Burney and John Thompson, seamen, the latter much bruised and injured. The accident is to be attributed to the very thick stale of the weather during the whole of yesterday, occasioning a mistake in the captains reckoning. A list of the passengers is subjoined : þÿ Lieutenant Shore, 14th Regiment' wife and four daughters, bodies not found, George Higginbottom, servant to the above, not found ; Walter 1'cmberton, Esq , of Nevis, not found ; Miss Pemberton, his daughter found; Miss Courley, of Portsmouth, not found, Mr. Shepherd, of Exeter, not lound ; five of the bodies of the crew have been cast ashore.

The .Marquis of Hertford, i he Sardanapalus of his caste, draws annually some sixty thousand pounds sterling from his estate in the north of Ireland, a single ducat of which never returns to that country. He hold sixty-four thousand þÿ green þÿacres in the county of Antrim ! The luxurious Marquis flies, at the approach of winter to the sun-lit shores of Italy and returns here as the spring advances, to share in the sensual enjoyments of the heart, less crowd of fashion, and to draw around him some hundreds of the tribe, at his splendid palazzo in the Regent's Park. Wealth reigns here supreme, and Hertford is the Lucullus of his day. His rent-roll, on the death of the Dowager Marchionness, was said to be over ninety-thousand a year ; and lie was residuary legatee to the Duke of Queensbury, whose natural daughter he married, and thus clutched more than half a-million sterling I þÿ The Marchioness has resided several years in Paris with her son, the heir to the marquisate and vast estates attached in England and Ireland ; the Marquis consoled himself in the platonic converse and society of a lady, since become thecara sposa of an Italian Marchesc; and thus þÿ all goes merry as a marriage bed! þÿ! At one of the Noble Marquis' balls, or felts, of the past week, we are told, by the fashionable Gazette, that cards were issued for more than twelve hundred, and that one thousand came and worshipped. His Highness of Orange was there, with a crowd of German Princes, and the orange flower was conspicu-

ous among the festoons and devices, in compliment to the heir of the mighty kingdom of Holland. The ball opened with the new and favourite þÿ gallopade'1 of þÿ þÿVarsovie þÿ which, we suppose, was composed to commemorate the hasty flight of his þÿHighness l s ate brother in-law Constantine, and his Russian mercenarties, from Warsaw, and was therefore a most appropriate þÿ gallopade þÿI Then we are told that Miss Strachan, the Marquis's þÿ proþÿtege, (how delicately touched,) danced a quadrille with one of the young Orange Princes; and that Madam Malibran, nr Dc Beriot was amongst the most animated in the waltzes. At two o'clock a most sumptuous supper was served, and morning had long dawned before the crowd dispersed. Let the Marquis of Hertford's tenanrv read the glowing account of this pageant, which probably cost some thousands, and think of their distresses no more ! Let them feast their eyes on þÿ the sumptuous þÿsupper, and revel in all the luxury of ideal enjoyment ! What arc municipal rights or tithes, when contrasted with such a scene ns this. Corporations may still flourish, and tithes. þÿ þÿ Well speeds alike the banquetand the þÿhall! The Noble Marquis reigns supreme in pomp and luxury. He is the Apicius of En gland and Italy ; and what more can the bogtrotters of Ireland, or the clodpoles of Suffolk, propably desire or want ? þÿ Sunday Times.

In England tranquility appears to prevail since the proroguation of Parliament. In France M. Mole is the new Prime Minister, his colleagues are M. Guizot , Persil, llosamel, $-c. Marshal Soult had positively declined taking any office in the new ministry, although earnestly urged to accept the ministry of war, by the King. In Spain much insubordination existed in the army þÿ many officers having been forced to resign by the mutinous disposition of the troops. M. Gomez, one of their generals had beaten and nearly annihilated 2,000 of the Queens troops under Lopez, the latter having been forced by his own soldiers, to fight treble his own number, under disadvantageous circumstances þÿ in consequence Gomez advanced within a few leagues of Madrid, spreading consternation in the capital. The King of Belgium had arrived in London The Emperor of Russia had issued an Ukase for the levy of 200,000 men to recruit (as it is said), his extensive armies. To roar a numerous pro- C geny J through & all the various stages, and finally set them forward in life, is unquestionably a task of considerable difficulty, and attended Ly no small degree of anxiety Vet if circumstances be not singularly unfavorable, so as to produce real trouble and sorrow, there can be no doubt that the effect of such a duty upon the mind is highly beneficial. The domestic relations, are of immense importance in developing and keeping awake the affections. We can scarcely be afflicted with hardness of heart towards any benign sentiment, if we have known what it was to be brother, husband and father. þÿ Women are peculiarly liable to he improved in general humanity by having children. When a mother of young infants passes a little child which has been neglected, upon the street, she cannot rest till she has seen it attended to ; the no childed would have never remarked the circumstance. When the mother of a set of roistering hoys passes a merry group of the same order, she is almost sorry that decorum will not allow her to linger beside them, to survey their sports, and bless them with a mother's blessing. If, advanced in life, she has seen some of her sons leave her for distant climes, should her path be crossed by the homeless vagrant, who looks, hut does not speak a petition, she thinks that there may have been, or still may be, some one to whom he is as interesting as her own child is to her þÿ or that her own child may one day appear to some other

mother as this wretch now appears to her and she extends to him the hand of melting charity. Thus does nature by an abundant flow of their finest sensations remunerate those whom she has called upon to perform what many calculating people would consider a disproportionate share of her duties.
